annotations.title: Jesus Christ
annotations.short: The Son of God, hungry after forty days, rests His head in His hand.
annotations.extended: Mark’s Gospel gives the scene two short verses: after his baptism, Christ was in the wilderness forty days, tempted by Satan, with the wild beasts, while angels served him. Moretto shows no struggle. Christ rests his head on his hand, a gesture long used in art for meditation and for melancholy.

more.story: He chose this weakness for us. He knows hunger and weariness from the inside, and He did not turn from either.

verses.text: Surely He took up our infirmities and carried our sorrows
we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin.

annotations.title: The Angels
annotations.short: Angels come from heaven to serve the Lord in His hunger.
annotations.extended: Mark and Matthew both end the wilderness story with angels attending Christ. Here two of them arrive in flight from the upper right.

more.story: Satan tempted Him with the promise of angels. He refused to test His Father, and the angels came anyway, as servants to their King.

verses.text: For He will command His angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways.
Then the devil left Him, and angels came and ministered to Him.

annotations.title: The Basilisk
annotations.short: A small dragon lies low near Him: a basilisk, the Met says.
annotations.extended: The Met calls it a small dragon or basilisk, and links it, with the lion and the serpent, to Psalm 91, the psalm Satan quotes to Christ during the temptation. The next verse in the Latin Bible of Moretto’s day reads, in an early English translation: “Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk: and thou shalt trample under foot the lion and the dragon.”

more.story: Moretto’s Bible promised that the faithful would tread on the basilisk. In Christ that promise is kept, and the serpent’s power over us is broken.

verses.text: Thou shalt walk upon the asp and the basilisk: and thou shalt trample under foot the lion and the dragon.
I have given you authority to tread on snakes and scorpions

annotations.title: The Lion
annotations.short: The lion, king of beasts, lies at the feet of the King of kings.
annotations.extended: Lions are among the wild beasts the Met identifies in the painting, and the Met links this one, with the serpent and the small dragon, to Psalm 91, which promises that the lion will be trampled. In Christian art the lion can stand for strength and kingship. Here it is calm, which suits a reading of the wilderness as a place where creation is at peace with Christ.

more.story: Daniel needed an angel to shut the lions’ mouths. This lion needs no angel. It knows its Lord and lies down.

verses.text: My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions.
Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed

annotations.title: The Stag
annotations.short: A stag bends toward Him, its head lowered.
annotations.extended: A stag crosses the slope at the left. The deer was a familiar Christian image of the soul seeking God, taken from Psalm 42. Whether Moretto meant that here, or simply painted the animals of a wild place, cannot be settled from the picture alone.

more.story: The psalmist longed for God as a deer longs for water. Here that longing has found Him. Whoever is thirsty may come.

verses.text: As the deer pants for streams of water, so my soul longs after You, O God.
If anyone is thirsty, let him come to Me and drink.

annotations.title: The Fox
annotations.short: A fox rests a few steps from Him.
annotations.extended: The Met’s subject tags list foxes among the painting’s animals. No single symbolic meaning fits them securely here; they belong, with the bear and the deer, to the wild beasts Mark says were with Christ.

more.story: Every creature on this hillside has a place to sleep. Their Maker had nowhere to lay His head, and He bore it for us.

verses.text: Through Him all things were made
Foxes have dens… but the Son of Man has no place to lay His head.

annotations.title: The Bear
annotations.short: A bear lies in the grass with its head bowed.
annotations.extended: The Met’s subject tags list bears among the painting’s animals, without saying which animal is meant; this one could also be read as a wild boar. Predators lying at rest near grazing animals recall Isaiah’s peaceable kingdom, where the wolf lives with the lamb and the bear feeds beside the cow. That echo is a reading, not something the painting states.

more.story: A man alone in these hills should fear a bear. With Jesus Christ, the wild is at peace, as Isaiah said it would be.

verses.text: The cow will graze with the bear, their young will lie down together
He was with the wild animals, and the angels ministered to Him.

annotations.title: The Missing Picture
annotations.short: Faint cherubs at the left edge, where the original canvas was cut away.
annotations.extended: The Met describes the canvas as a fragment of a larger work that once continued past the sketchy cherubim at the left and showed other events from Christ’s life. It has been suggested that Moretto’s Christ Blessing Saint John the Baptist, now in London, came from the same composition, though the National Gallery notes that the figures differ in scale.

more.story: This was once part of a larger painting of His life. His story continues past the frame, to the cross and the empty tomb.

verses.text: There are many more things that Jesus did.

annotations.title: The White Bird
annotations.short: A long-necked white bird bends low beside Him.
annotations.extended: No source names this bird, and with its long neck, dagger bill and long legs it looks more like a heron or egret than a pelican. Christians long took the pelican as a sign of Christ’s sacrifice; whether Moretto meant anything of the kind here is unknown.

more.story: The psalmist, alone in his grief, called himself a bird of the wilderness. Christians later saw in the pelican, said to feed its young with its own blood, a picture of Christ, who gave His life for us.

verses.text: I am become like to a pelican of the wilderness
Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends.

annotations.title: The Serpent at His Feet
annotations.short: A thin serpent slips beneath His bare foot.
annotations.extended: A thin serpent on the rock below Christ’s foot. The Met links it, with the lion, to Psalm 91:13, where the faithful tread on lion and serpent. It also recalls God’s promise in Genesis 3:15.

more.story: God promised in Eden that the serpent would strike the heel and have its head crushed. Here the heel rests above it, unafraid.

verses.text: He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel.
The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet.

annotations.title: The Beech
annotations.short: A beech rises over Him, green and red against the sky.
annotations.extended: The Met identifies the tree as a beech: an attribute of Christ, and a sign of abstinence, because hermits were said to live on its nuts. Seeing it also as the tree of the cross is a reading, not something the Met states.
references: The Met, “Botanical Imagery in European Painting”

more.story: Adam lost the tree of life in Eden. One day Jesus Christ would carry our sins on a tree, to open the way back.

verses.text: In the middle of the garden were the tree of life
He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree

annotations.title: The Raven
annotations.short: A black bird, perhaps a raven, pecks at the top of the rock.
annotations.extended: No source names this bird; it looks like a raven or a crow. In Scripture ravens are the wilderness’s providers: God sent them to feed Elijah, and legend says a raven brought the hermit Paul his bread. Whether Moretto meant that here is unknown.

more.story: God fed Elijah in the wilderness by ravens, morning and evening. The One who feeds the ravens sits here hungry, and trusts His Father.

verses.text: The ravens would bring him bread and meat in the morning and evening
Consider the ravens: They do not sow or reap… yet God feeds them.

annotations.title: The Animal on the Rocks
annotations.short: An animal comes down the rocks with its head lowered, perhaps a second bear.
annotations.extended: No source names this animal. Large and brown, with a rounded back and heavy legs, it may be a second bear, or a wolf. It belongs to the wild beasts Mark says were with Christ in the wilderness.

more.story: Every beast of the forest belongs to God. This one comes down the rocks toward its Maker, and is not afraid.

verses.text: For every beast of the forest is Mine—the cattle on a thousand hills.
He was with the wild animals, and the angels ministered to Him.
